published_title: THE COUGH THAT FOLLOWED THE BELLS

story.title: THE COUGH THAT FOLLOWED THE BELLS
story.deck: Forty-one children cough every Sunday night in a mountain town that has spent five weeks blaming its doctors and its church, and nobody has asked which bell, which room, or what changed last winter.
story.shape: A diagnosis in six scenes: a reframe from address to bed, a test built to lose, a sweep and a ringer and a mother's notebook that each hold part of the answer and a veto, and a descent that finds the pressure no one was looking for.

scenes.title: Forty-One Notebooks
paragraphs: *Children's clinic, Ostrava Vell · Monday, 07:40*
Ostrava Vell was a mountain town of four thousand people, one church with a tower too large for it, and, since the second week of September, forty-one children who coughed in the evenings.
Dr. Ilse Varga had taped her spirometry curves to the examination-room wall, one line to a child. Every line sagged on Sunday night and climbed back by Thursday, forty-one small tides.

**Ilse Varga**  
Cultures, PCR, serology, three rounds. There is nothing in any of them. No virus I know keeps a calendar.
Judit Moravec, who chaired the town council, had come in with her coat on and meant to leave in it. Father Matej Hroch of St. Wenzel stood by the door with his hands folded in his sleeves.

**Judit Moravec**  
The council wants the school shut on Wednesday. A closed school is a thing I can actually do. Tell me what else I can do by Wednesday and I will do that instead.

**Ilse Varga**  
I can tell you that it costs the fifteen-year-olds their exams in six weeks, and that I cannot promise it helps.

**Matej Hroch**  
And while you are all looking for something to shut, leave the bells out of it. This town blamed them for the hail, the frost and the winter the cows failed. They were innocent every time.

Illuminara had been asked to read the evidence rather than the people. She stood a while before the curves, then before the map beside them, where each child was a pin in the street they lived on and the pins thickened toward the church.

**Illuminara**  
Everyone has plotted the children by where they live. Has anyone plotted them by where they sleep?

**Ilse Varga**  
Where they sleep is where they live.

**Illuminara**  
Usually.
Nives Hadzic had come in with her coat still buttoned. She held out a school exercise book, soft at the corners.

**Nives Hadzic**  
Forty-one mothers, forty-one notebooks. You asked for them in week two, Doctor. I write down every cough and the hour. And Lenka does not fit. We are out on Spindle Road, past the cemetery, the farthest house from the tower there is. She coughs on Sundays like the rest of them.

**Ilse Varga**  
I set Lenka aside as an outlier.
Illuminara turned the pages. *Saturday: to Baba's. Sunday: home at five. Sunday night: coughing, two hours.*

**Illuminara**  
Where is Baba's?

**Nives Hadzic**  
Cooper's Lane. Right under the tower, near enough.

**Illuminara**  
Then she is not an outlier. She is the one child you have who proves something. The cough follows the child and not the address, so it is not a house or a street, and probably not a germ going door to door. It is a room she slept in, and the room has a clock.
*The doctors had asked what was in the children. Nobody had asked what was in the rooms.*

**Judit Moravec**  
And the school?

**Illuminara**  
Tell me which of these children sleep there.

scenes.title: Saint's Flour
paragraphs: *St. Wenzel's tower, ringing chamber · Monday, 10:15*

The ringing chamber smelled of rope and cold stone. Dana Kral had pulled the bells of St. Wenzel for thirty-eight years, as her husband had before her, and she watched the stranger look at the ropes instead of the bells and made ready to be annoyed.

**Illuminara**  
I have one question, and I think nobody has asked it. Which bell is the heaviest, and when is it rung?

**Dana Kral**  
Everybody asks which is loudest.

**Illuminara**  
I am not asking about loud.

**Dana Kral**  
Old Wenzel. Two tonnes and a hundred kilos. Four of us swing him, Sundays and feast days only. The little ones go from the keyboard, and the hour bells strike by the clock, every day of the week.

**Matej Hroch**  
There, you see. The hour bells strike every day and nobody coughs on a Tuesday.

**Illuminara**  
I agree. So it is not the bells. It may be one bell, on one day.

She asked for a single stroke of the old bell. Hroch looked a long time at the rope, and allowed exactly one. Dana and three ringers swung Old Wenzel up from rest, and Illuminara went down to the ground chamber and stood on the flagstones at the west wall.

The stroke came through the tower like a blow to the bottom of a chair. She had never needed her ears for a bell. The tower pressed its weight into the stone, the stone passed it down, and she read where the paths ran. Under the west wall they stopped. There was one place where the rock no longer carried anything and only hung, a long emptiness with a thin roof, and it answered the stroke the way a drumhead answers a palm.
*Something down there rings.*

**Illuminara**  
Under this wall there is a hollow, wide and shallow, with a thin ceiling over it. When Old Wenzel strikes, the ceiling moves.

**Matej Hroch**  
The tower stands on rock.

**Dana Kral**  
It stands on the lip of the old adit. The miners' air shaft, bricked and boarded before my grandmother's time. Mind the floor by the lectern, it is hollow.
She pushed back her sleeve. Along the dark wool lay a fine white powder, like flour.

**Dana Kral**  
Saint's flour. It comes up between the boards on every feast day. Ringers have worn it for three hundred years. My grandmother said it was Wenzel blessing our hands.

**Illuminara**  
Then it is not new. Something else is.

**Emil Rask**  
I can tell you what is new.
The chimney sweep had come up the tower stairs behind them with his apprentice and a bag of rods. He was sixty-eight years old and filled the doorway.

**Emil Rask**  
Last winter's grant. I did sixty-three chimneys for it in the old quarter. New stoves, sealed windows, no draught, less coal. I told the council what I tell everyone. A house with its windows shut drinks from its cellar.

**Dana Kral**  
And did the council listen?

**Emil Rask**  
They liked the part about the coal.
*A bell that had rung for three hundred years, and a grant that had saved sixty-three households a winter's fuel. Neither dangerous alone.*

scenes.title: Two Mouths
paragraphs: *Cooper's Lane, cellars of the old quarter · Tuesday, 14:00*
Emil Rask had one rule for entering a cellar and he gave it on every doorstep: the tenant says yes, or the rods stay in the bag.
Eleven of the twelve said yes. Alois Fenner, at number nine, stood in his doorway with his arms folded.

**Alois Fenner**  
My father's cellar and his father's. Nobody counts my air.

**Emil Rask**  
Then I cannot map it, Alois. Not without you.

**Alois Fenner**  
Then don't.
Illuminara could have found the mouth of that cellar in half a minute. She looked at the sweep, and at the folded arms, and left the cellar unread. The map would have a gap in it.

In Baba Hadzic's cellar the apprentice, Tilo, who was sixteen and had been told to say nothing, lit a smoke pencil by the coal bin and held it to the wall. The thread of smoke lay over and leaned toward a bricked arch behind the bin, where the mortar was thin enough to feel a cold breath through.

**Tilo**  
It is pulling in. All of it, here.
The sweep took the pencil to a grating in the cellar's other wall. The smoke leaned that way too.

**Emil Rask**  
Two mouths. Don't you tell me it is one. The arch feeds this room, and so does the street.

**Illuminara**  
I won't. The street air should be nearly clean and the arch should not, but I cannot claim either until something counts them. If I am wrong about the arch, a stove on a Tuesday would be breathing what a stove breathes on a Sunday.
Ilse Varga had arrived with three laser dust counters in a padded case.

**Ilse Varga**  
Nobody says the word silica in my clinic until a counter says particles.

**Illuminara**  
Agreed. Then a test that can lose. Wednesday at three, when no one is baking and no one is at church. Counters in three cellars: Baba Hadzic's, one at the school on the far edge, one down the lane. Ten minutes of the small bells only. Then Old Wenzel alone, for ten.

**Illuminara**  
If the school's counter climbs with Baba's, the dust is in the air everywhere and I am wrong. If the small bells raise Baba's, it is the tower and not the shaft, and I am wrong again. If Baba's has not at least quadrupled within twenty minutes of the first stroke, I am wrong a third way.

**Ilse Varga**  
And if you are right?

**Illuminara**  
Then we still do not know what the dust is. That needs a lab.

**Emil Rask**  
And I want the grating counted by itself. A counter in the pipe.

**Illuminara**  
You shall have one.

scenes.title: Wednesday, Out of Season
paragraphs: *St. Wenzel's tower and three cellars · Wednesday, 15:00*
Nobody could order Old Wenzel rung. Four ringers swung him by their own wish or not at all, and the wish was Dana Kral's.

**Dana Kral**  
I will ring him on a Wednesday, which I have never done, for ten minutes, which I have never wanted. If one telephone call comes from the clinic with a child's name in it, I stop on the spot, and I do not care what is on your counters.

**Matej Hroch**  
And I will stand in my tower and watch you do it.

The mothers had decided among themselves that no child should be in the old quarter's cellars that afternoon. Nives Hadzic had chalked it on the schoolyard gate. Ilse Varga read the counters over the telephone from the clinic.

**Ilse Varga**  
Baseline, all three: Baba Hadzic's twenty-two, the school nineteen, Cooper's Lane twenty-four. Stoves are lit, same as any weekday. Small bells, now.
The five small bells chimed for ten minutes, bright and a little silly in the dry air.

**Ilse Varga**  
Twenty-one. Twenty. Twenty-four. Nothing.

**Matej Hroch**  
The bells are innocent.

**Illuminara**  
The small ones are. Dana.
Four ringers, one rope, and Old Wenzel went up from rest and spoke. The note was lower than anything the ear could hold. It lived in the soles of the feet.

**Ilse Varga**  
Minute four. Baba Hadzic's thirty-one. School nineteen.

**Ilse Varga**  
Minute eight. Eighty-eight. School twenty.
Hroch was looking at his sleeves. Between the boards the saint's flour rose in a thin white breath.

**Dana Kral**  
Ten minutes. That was the bargain.
She let the rope settle. The dust in the lane was still on its way, and the counters kept climbing after the bell had stopped.

**Ilse Varga**  
Minute fourteen. A hundred and ninety. School nineteen. Cooper's Lane a hundred and twelve. The pipe from the street grating, twenty-six.
Nobody spoke for a while. The arch had fed that cellar nearly nine times its ordinary dust, and the street had hardly stirred it.

**Matej Hroch**  
It may be my tower's own stone. Limestone dusts. Pigeons. I will not be told it is the shaft until somebody looks at what the dust is.

**Illuminara**  
That is the right objection.

**Ilse Varga**  
The tower is limestone, and limestone will not hurt a child's lung. Quartz will. If I find quartz in this, it is not your tower. If I find lime and pigeon, I will tell the council the bells were blamed wrongly again, Father, and I will say it from your pulpit if you let me.

**Matej Hroch**  
I will let you.

scenes.title: One Course of Brick
paragraphs: *The old air shaft and the adit beneath the west wall · Thursday, 06:00*
Hroch had allowed one course of brick to be lifted from the tower floor, and had asked that it be put back. Under the brick was a shaft a metre wide, plastered smooth, falling into the dark.
Emil Rask would let no one go down it. He had put a torch on the timbers below and said what he thought of them.

**Emil Rask**  
That roof has been rotting since my grandfather's day. Anything that goes down there goes down on a rope, and I would be burying it.

**Illuminara**  
I do not need the rope. I do need you on the cable. Tell me every ten minutes what the counter on my lanyard says, and tell me when to stop talking. I stop answering when I am working.

**Emil Rask**  
If the roof comes down on you, am I to dig?

**Illuminara**  
No. Wait. I will be a while, and I will come back.

She went down into a dark that was a kind of information. The gallery ran a hundred and forty metres under Cooper's Lane, low enough that a man would have stooped. The roof was lined with lime plaster as thick as a hand, mixed with sharp white sand. In places it had come away from the rock and hung in sheets, like slate on a wet wall. On the floor lay three centimetres of dust the colour of flour. Where she stepped it rose and stayed in the air like a held breath.

**Illuminara**  
The counter says eleven hundred where I stand. The plaster over me is six centimetres thick and unbonded on the west side. The arch to Cooper's Lane is sixty-two metres east, the one you smoked. The street grating's branch joins at forty metres and its air is clean, as you said.

**Emil Rask**  
Told you it was fed from both.

**Illuminara**  
You did. It carries about a tenth of it. I will say so at the table.

She took three samples in glass: roof plaster, floor dust, and a flake of the tower's own limestone she had brought down for comparison. It would have been easy to feel certain now. She made herself wait for the lab.

There was one thing she had not expected, and it mattered more than the sampling. The bell did not arrive in the gallery only as shaking. It arrived as pressure. Every stroke pumped the long tunnel like a bellows, shoving air down the shaft and drawing it back, and each pump drove the dust east along the floor toward the arch.

**Illuminara**  
Emil. If you plug that arch, the plug needs a breather. A pipe from the gallery to the open air, a long way from any window. Otherwise the bell will press the dust through the old mortar around whatever you build, like water through a sponge.

**Emil Rask**  
That is what a chimney sweep is for, miss. I would have said so in the next minute.

**Illuminara**  
Say it in this one.

**Emil Rask**  
A pipe along the cemetery wall, to a stub chimney above the roofline. Thirty metres. Tilo can lay it by Saturday.

Then she worked. The tunnel was too long and too rotten to save in a morning, and she did not pretend otherwise. She read where the plaster would let go first, under the bell's footprint, and there she sprayed a lime-and-casein binder from the hose Tilo fed down the shaft, a skin that would hold the sand until spring and a proper crew. Eleven metres. It took four hours.

**Illuminara**  
A hundred and twenty-nine metres remain untouched. The worst of it is covered. It is not all of it. I want that written down.

**Emil Rask**  
It is written.
The lab result reached the clinic on Friday morning, and Ilse read it down the telephone in her flattest voice.

**Ilse Varga**  
Angular quartz, three to eight microns, in a lime binder. The same as your gallery plaster. No quartz in the tower limestone. No pigeon. Father, your stone is clean.

scenes.title: The Full Peal
paragraphs: *Piazza of St. Wenzel · Sunday, 11:00*

By Saturday night the arch had a plug of lime brick and a breather pipe that ran thirty metres along the cemetery wall to a stub chimney above the roofline. The tower floor was sealed. Alois Fenner's cellar had needed no entering at all: with the arch closed on the gallery side, it drew its air from the street grating, which was clean, and he had never had to open his door.
Dana Kral stood at the rope with three ringers. Counters were live in four cellars and Ilse Varga was on the telephone in the clinic.

**Dana Kral**  
He will go at three-quarter swing, not full, until the gallery is relined. Seventy strokes and not ninety. I will miss the old swing. The bell will not mind.

**Matej Hroch**  
The parish will pay for the cap on the shaft. I have said so to the council, and they have agreed, and the grant is amended: no stove goes into a house in this town again until Emil has put a smoke pencil to its cellar.

**Judit Moravec**  
The school stays open. I would like it minuted that I was told it would.

Old Wenzel went up and spoke. People stopped in the square with their faces lifted, because the old note was in their feet again, and a little way off Alois Fenner stood in his doorway with his arms folded and said to nobody that it was too loud.

**Ilse Varga**  
Minute six. Baba Hadzic's twenty-two. Minute twelve, twenty-three. Minute eighteen, twenty-five. School nineteen.
No white breath rose between the boards. Dana looked at her sleeve, clean to the elbow, and was quiet a moment.

**Dana Kral**  
I miss it.

**Illuminara**  
Keep a pinch in a jar. It is a record, not a blessing now. It tells you what the tower did for three hundred years, and what it will do again if the plaster is let go.

Lenka Hadzic had gone to Baba's on Saturday night, as she had every Saturday of her life, and slept in the room under the tower. Ilse brought the spirometer to Cooper's Lane at six that evening and again at half past seven on Monday morning, and the line did not sag.
Nives Hadzic sat at Baba's kitchen table and opened the exercise book to the last page. She wrote the day, and the hour, and under it she wrote what she had waited five weeks to write.
*Sunday night: Lenka asleep. No cough.*

story.title: THE COUGH THAT FOLLOWED THE BELLS
story.deck: Forty-one children cough every Sunday night in a mountain town that has spent five weeks blaming its doctors and its church, and nobody has asked which bell, which room, or what changed last winter.
story.shape: A diagnosis in six scenes: a reframe from address to bed, a test built to lose, a sweep and a ringer and a mother's notebook that each hold part of the answer and a veto, a descent that finds the pressure no one was looking for, and a cohort check, a commissioning peal and a standing rule that keep the result honest.

scenes.title: Forty-One Notebooks
paragraphs: *Children's clinic, Ostrava Vell · Monday, 07:40*
Ostrava Vell was a mountain town of four thousand people, one church with a tower too large for it, and, since the second week of September, forty-one children who coughed in the evenings.
Dr. Ilse Varga had taped her spirometry curves to the examination-room wall, one line to a child. Every line sagged on Sunday night and climbed back by Thursday, forty-one small tides.

**Ilse Varga**  
Cultures, PCR, serology, three rounds. There is nothing in any of them. No virus I know keeps a calendar.
Judit Moravec, who chaired the town council, had come in with her coat on. Father Matej Hroch of St. Wenzel stood by the door with his hands in his sleeves.

**Judit Moravec**  
The council wants the school shut on Wednesday. A closed school is a thing I can actually do. Tell me what else I can do by Wednesday.

**Matej Hroch**  
While you look for something to shut, leave the bells out of it. This town blamed them for the hail and the winter the cows failed. They were innocent every time.
Illuminara stood before the curves, then before the map beside them, where each child was a pin in the street they lived on and the pins thickened toward the church.

**Illuminara**  
Everyone has plotted the children by where they live. Has anyone plotted them by where they sleep?

**Ilse Varga**  
Where they sleep is where they live.

**Illuminara**  
Usually.
Nives Hadzic had come in with her coat still buttoned. She held out a school exercise book, soft at the corners.

**Nives Hadzic**  
Forty-one mothers, forty-one notebooks. I write down every cough, the hour, and where she slept that night. And Lenka does not fit. We are out on Spindle Road, past the cemetery, the farthest house from the tower there is. She coughs on Sundays like the rest of them.

**Ilse Varga**  
I set Lenka aside as an outlier.
Illuminara turned the pages. *Saturday: to Baba's on Cooper's Lane. Sunday: home at five. Sunday night: coughing, two hours.*

**Illuminara**  
Cooper's Lane is right under the tower. Then she is not an outlier. She is the one child you have who proves something. The cough follows the child and not the address, so it is not a street, and probably not a germ going door to door. It is a room she slept in, and the room has a clock.
*The doctors had asked what was in the children. Nobody had asked what was in the rooms.*

**Illuminara**  
Tell me where each of them slept on Saturday night.

scenes.title: Saint's Flour
paragraphs: *St. Wenzel's tower, ringing chamber · Monday, 10:15*
Dana Kral had pulled the bells of St. Wenzel for thirty-eight years, as her husband had before her, and she watched the stranger look at the ropes instead of the bells and made ready to be annoyed.

**Illuminara**  
I have one question, and I think nobody has asked it. Which bell is the heaviest, and when is it rung?

**Dana Kral**  
Everybody asks which is loudest.

**Illuminara**  
I am not asking about loud.

**Dana Kral**  
Old Wenzel, two tonnes and a hundred kilos. Four of us swing him, Sundays and feast days only. The little ones go from the keyboard, and the hour bells strike by the clock every day.

**Matej Hroch**  
There, you see. The hour bells strike every day and nobody coughs on a Tuesday.

**Illuminara**  
I agree. So it is not the bells. It may be one bell, on one day.

She asked for a single stroke of the old bell. Hroch looked a long time at the rope, and allowed exactly one. Dana and three ringers swung Old Wenzel up, and Illuminara went down and stood on the flagstones at the west wall.

The stroke came through the tower like a blow to the bottom of a chair. The tower pressed its weight into the stone, the stone passed it down, and she read where the paths ran. Under the west wall they stopped. There the rock carried nothing and only hung, a long emptiness with a thin roof, and it answered the stroke the way a drumhead answers a palm.
*Something down there rings.*

**Illuminara**  
Under this wall there is a hollow, wide and shallow. When Old Wenzel strikes, its ceiling moves.

**Matej Hroch**  
The tower stands on rock.

**Dana Kral**  
It stands on the lip of the old adit. The miners' air shaft, bricked and boarded before my grandmother's time. Mind the floor by the lectern, it is hollow.
She pushed back her sleeve. Along the dark wool lay a fine white powder, like flour.

**Dana Kral**  
Saint's flour. It comes up between the boards on every feast day. My grandmother said it was Wenzel blessing our hands.

**Illuminara**  
Then it is not new. Something else is.

**Emil Rask**  
I can tell you what is new.
The chimney sweep had come up the stairs behind them with his apprentice and a bag of rods. He was sixty-eight and filled the doorway.

**Emil Rask**  
Last winter's grant. I did sixty-three chimneys for it in the old quarter. New stoves, sealed windows, no draught, less coal. A house with its windows shut drinks from its cellar.

scenes.title: Two Mouths
paragraphs: *Cooper's Lane, cellars of the old quarter · Tuesday, 14:00*
Emil Rask had one rule for entering a cellar and he gave it on every doorstep: the tenant says yes, or the rods stay in the bag.
Eleven of the twelve said yes. Alois Fenner, at number nine, stood in his doorway with his arms folded.

**Alois Fenner**  
My father's cellar and his father's. Nobody counts my air.

**Emil Rask**  
Then I cannot map it, Alois. Not without you.

**Alois Fenner**  
Then don't.

**Tilo**  
It is pulling in. All of it.
The sweep took the pencil to a grating in the cellar's other wall. The smoke leaned that way too.

**Emil Rask**

**Illuminara**

**Ilse Varga**  
Nobody says the word silica in my clinic until a counter says particles.

**Illuminara**

**Ilse Varga**  
And if you are right, you still do not know what the dust is.

**Illuminara**  
No. That needs a lab.

**Emil Rask**  
And I want the grating counted by itself. A counter in the pipe.

**Illuminara**  
You shall have one.

The mothers had decided that no child should be in the old quarter's cellars that afternoon. Ilse Varga read the counters over the telephone from the clinic.

Twenty-one. Twenty. Twenty-four. Nothing.

**Illuminara**

**Ilse Varga**  
Minute four. Baba Hadzic's thirty-one. School nineteen.

The arch had fed that cellar nearly nine times its ordinary dust, and the street had hardly stirred it.

**Illuminara**  
That is the right objection.

**Ilse Varga**

**Matej Hroch**  
I will let you.
